headline: The Hockey Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet teammates, give numbers and times, describe your gear and the ice, ask simple questions, make polite requests at the rink, and start Hockey Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Say hockey gear words clearly and greet teammates and coaches at the rink.
lessons.focus: The five pure vowels, ch, j, ll, rr and the written accent in rink and gear words

words.note: Said JO-kei: in this borrowed word the h sounds like Spanish j.
The h is silent; hie sounds like English ye: YEH-lo.
Spanish vowels are short and pure: a as in father, o as in note.
Mexican word. ch sounds like ch in church; rr is a strong rolled r.
j sounds like a strong English h. A woman is la jugadora.
ll sounds like English y in yes: ro-di-YEH-ra.
An r at the start of a word is rolled, like rr.
rr is a trilled r; compare pero (but) and perro (dog).
The written accent marks the stressed syllable: AR-bi-tro.
Common word in Mexico and the US.

words.en: My name is Sam, nice to meet you.

words.note: Informal tú, between teammates. To a coach or referee, use the formal ¿Cómo está?

words.en: How do you say "puck" in Spanish?

lessons.speaking: Greet a teammate in the locker room, say your name, and ask how to say one piece of your gear in Spanish.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Give your jersey number, gear sizes, practice times and the score in Spanish.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time with a las, and hockey quantities: periods, minutes, inches, pounds

words.note: Also used for your jersey number; put el before the digits.
Also written período; both spellings are correct.
Also used to ask the clock time; say a las before the time.
Also means the scoreboard.
Many players in the US also say el puck.
For skates, many people also say el número.
Many people in Mexico and the US also say la práctica.
In the US, stick length is measured in inches.
In the US, body weight and gear weight are given in pounds.

words.en: Each period is 15 minutes, according to the league.
words.es: Cada periodo es de 15 minutos, según la liga.
words.note: Period length depends on the league; use de with measurements.

lessons.speaking: Tell the coach your jersey number, your skate size, and what time practice starts.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Say who people on the team are and describe your gear, the ice and how you feel.
lessons.focus: ser for who someone is (soy, es); estar for conditions and location (estoy, está)

words.note: A woman coach is la entrenadora.
Also means the gear, as in hockey gear.
A woman goalie is la portera.
Use estar for ready; with ser it means clever. A woman says lista.
Use estar. A woman says cansada.
Use estar. A woman says lastimada.
Used for skate blades, with estar.
Use estar; it agrees with the noun (abierta).
Use estar; it agrees with the noun (cerrada).
A woman says nueva.
ser: who you are. A woman says nueva.

words.en: The coach is in the locker room.
words.es: El entrenador está en el vestidor.
words.note: estar: location.
estar: a condition that can change.

words.es: Ella es la portera del equipo.

lessons.speaking: Tell the coach whether you are ready, tired or hurt, whether your skates are sharpened, and where your gear is.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Say what gear you have, what is missing and what you need in the locker room.
lessons.focus: tengo/tienes, hay, necesito, quiero and hay que + infinitive with gear words

words.note: Many players also say el bastón or el stick.
Mexican and US word, used for the bucket of pucks.
Common in Mexico and the US; some people say la camiseta.

words.en: There's no water on the bench.
words.es: No hay agua en la banca.
words.note: hay stays the same for one thing or many things.

words.en: I need tape for my stick.
I want to change my laces.
You have to wear the mouthguard.
words.es: Hay que usar el protector bucal.
words.note: hay que + infinitive: a general must, for everyone.
Informal tú, between teammates.

lessons.speaking: Ask a teammate in the locker room for tape or laces, and say what gear you have and what you still need.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Say where you are going, what you are going to do, and ask if you can go on the ice.
lessons.focus: ir and ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer for activities, and poder for can

words.note: Mexican word for the team bench.
In Mexico many people also say el camión.
Also the bench door.

words.en: I'm going to the gym after the game.
words.es: Voy al gimnasio después del partido.
words.note: a + el becomes al.

words.en: We're going to do the warm-up now.
words.es: Vamos a hacer el calentamiento ahora.

words.en: Can I go on the ice?
I'm going to arrive early tomorrow.
Today we're doing passes and shots.
The bus is going to leave at 5:00.
words.es: El autobús va a salir a las 5:00.

lessons.speaking: Tell a teammate where you are going after practice and what you are going to do tomorrow, then ask the coach if you can go on the ice.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Talk about your weekly hockey routine and ask teammates about theirs.
lessons.focus: Present tense of regular -ar, -er, -ir verbs: patino, patinas, patina, patinamos, patinan

words.note: A woman is la compañera.
A woman is la aficionada.
With los, it means every Monday.
Saying en la mañana for in the morning is common in Mexico and the US.
In Mexico, the main midday meal; also food in general.

words.en: I train on Mondays and Wednesdays.
words.es: Entreno los lunes y los miércoles.

words.note: Informal tú, between teammates.

words.en: We practice shots in the morning.
words.es: Nosotros practicamos tiros en la mañana.

words.en: They eat pasta before the game.
words.es: Ellos comen pasta antes del partido.

words.en: I receive the pass and shoot.
Do you live near the rink?
words.note: Formal usted, for a coach or a parent.

lessons.speaking: Tell a new teammate which days you train and what you eat before a game, then ask when they skate.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask teammates and coaches simple questions about people, places and times at the rink.
lessons.focus: Question words qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál with rising intonation

words.note: For more than one person, use quiénes.
Agrees with the noun it counts (cuántos, cuántas).
Alone, it also means Sorry, what did you say?
Two words for why; porque, one word, means because.
Use it to pick one from a group.
A woman is la capitana.

words.en: How much does it cost to sharpen skates?

lessons.speaking: Ask a teammate where the locker room is, who the captain is, and when the next game is.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say no, never, nobody, not yet, more, less and another about gear and play.
lessons.focus: no before the verb, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, and más, menos, otro

words.note: Before the verb, no extra no is needed.
After the verb, put no before the verb too.
After the verb, put no before the verb too.
Keep the written accent when it means more.
Never put un before otro.
Yo tampoco means Me neither.

words.es: No hay nadie en la banca.

words.en: I never skate without a helmet.

words.note: A woman says lista.

lessons.speaking: Tell the coach you are not ready yet, that you need another stick, and that you never skate without a helmet.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Ask coaches and staff politely for help and give simple usted commands at the rink.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede + infinitive? and usted commands: traiga, espere, hable, abra

words.note: The reply is de nada (you're welcome).
Say it to get past someone on the bench or in the locker room.
Use it to apologize or to get someone's attention.
Usted command, polite for a coach, staff or parent.

words.en: Can you pass me the tape?

words.es: Traiga la bolsa de hielo, por favor.

words.en: Can you open the locker room, please?

lessons.speaking: Ask the equipment manager politely to open the locker room and pass you tape, then ask them to speak more slowly.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Spot Spanish words you already know and get help when you don't understand at the rink.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad, -ente and survival phrases for getting help

words.note: The ending -dad often matches English -ty, as in velocity.
The ending -ción matches English -tion; these words are feminine.
In the US, call 911 in an emergency.
The ending -ente matches English -ent; same form for men and women.
Shout ¡Ayuda! to call for help.

words.en: I don't understand, can you help me?
Communication is very important on the ice.
words.es: La comunicación es muy importante en el hielo.

words.note: llamen is the plural command, to everyone around you.

lessons.speaking: Tell a teammate you don't understand, ask what a word means, and praise their pass or speed with a cognate.
